questions.question: What is the fundamental data structure underlying Kafka?
options: A hash table distributed across brokers
An append-only, immutable, ordered log
A B-tree index for fast lookups
A priority queue sorted by message importance
questions.explanation: Kafka is built on the append-only log abstraction. Messages are immutable once written, appended sequentially, and read by offset. This simple structure enables high throughput and natural ordering.

questions.question: Why are Kafka topics split into partitions?
options: To encrypt messages separately for different consumers
To enable parallel writes and reads, scaling throughput horizontally
To reduce the size of individual messages
To automatically compress data on disk
questions.explanation: Partitions allow Kafka to parallelize both writes (multiple producers can write to different partitions simultaneously) and reads (multiple consumers can read different partitions concurrently), enabling horizontal scaling.

questions.question: What does 'acks=all' mean for a Kafka producer?
options: The producer does not wait for any acknowledgment
Only the partition leader must acknowledge the write
All in-sync replicas must acknowledge the write before the producer considers it successful
All consumers must acknowledge they received the message
questions.explanation: With acks=all, the producer waits for all in-sync replicas (ISR) to confirm the write. This provides the strongest durability guarantee — the message survives even if the leader immediately crashes after acknowledging.

questions.question: In a consumer group, how are partitions assigned to consumers?
options: Each message is broadcast to all consumers in the group
Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, ensuring parallel non-overlapping processing
Consumers randomly pick partitions on each poll
All consumers read from all partitions simultaneously
questions.explanation: In a consumer group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer. This ensures that messages in a partition are processed in order by a single consumer, while the group as a whole processes partitions in parallel.

questions.question: What is the In-Sync Replica (ISR) set in Kafka?
options: All brokers in the Kafka cluster regardless of state
The set of replicas that are fully caught up with the partition leader
A backup of the consumer group's offset positions
A list of topics that share the same replication factor
questions.explanation: The ISR is the set of replicas (including the leader) that have fully replicated all messages from the leader. If a follower falls too far behind, it's removed from the ISR. Only ISR members are eligible for leader election.

questions.question: A Kafka topic has 6 partitions and a consumer group has 8 consumers. What happens?
options: Each consumer gets approximately 0.75 partitions using fractional assignment
Six consumers each get one partition; two consumers sit idle
Messages are duplicated so all consumers stay busy
The consumer group rejects the extra consumers with an error
questions.explanation: Each partition can only be assigned to one consumer in a group. With 8 consumers and 6 partitions, 6 consumers each get one partition and 2 consumers remain idle. Adding more consumers than partitions wastes resources.

questions.question: How does Kafka guarantee message ordering?
options: Messages are globally ordered across all partitions in a topic
Ordering is guaranteed within a single partition but not across partitions
Messages are sorted by timestamp after being written
Consumers sort messages in memory before processing
questions.explanation: Kafka guarantees ordering only within a single partition. Messages with the same partition key go to the same partition, ensuring they're consumed in order. There is no ordering guarantee across different partitions.

questions.question: What problem does Kafka's idempotent producer solve?
options: It prevents consumers from reading the same message twice
It ensures that retried produces don't create duplicate messages in the log
It encrypts messages before writing them to the partition
It compresses messages for faster network transfer
questions.explanation: Network failures can cause a producer to retry a write without knowing if the original succeeded. An idempotent producer assigns each message a sequence number, allowing the broker to detect and discard duplicates from retries.

questions.question: How does Kafka achieve exactly-once semantics end-to-end (producer to consumer)?
options: By using TCP which guarantees exactly-once delivery at the network layer
By combining idempotent producers, transactional writes, and atomic offset commits
By having consumers acknowledge every single message individually
Kafka cannot achieve exactly-once semantics — it only supports at-least-once
questions.explanation: Exactly-once requires: (1) idempotent producers to prevent duplicate writes, (2) transactions to atomically write messages and commit consumer offsets, and (3) read-committed isolation on the consumer side. All three work together.

questions.question: A Kafka cluster has a topic with replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas=2. The leader and one follower are up; one follower is down. A producer sends with acks=all. What happens?
options: The write fails because not all 3 replicas can acknowledge
The write succeeds because 2 in-sync replicas (leader + 1 follower) meet the min.insync.replicas requirement
The write is queued until the third replica recovers
The topic is automatically repartitioned to exclude the failed broker
questions.explanation: With acks=all, the producer needs acknowledgment from all ISR members. The ISR currently has 2 members (leader + 1 follower), which meets min.insync.replicas=2. The write succeeds. If another follower went down, the ISR would shrink to 1, which is below min.insync.replicas, and writes would be rejected.
